column2: Tamponade raises all diastolic pressures, so the JVP is high (blunted y descent); a collapsed JVP means hypovolaemia. Beck's triad: hypotension, raised JVP, quiet heart sounds.
Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (within weeks of surgery) is mostly coagulase-negative staphylococci or S. aureus acquired peri-operatively.
Constriction causes systemic congestion (raised JVP, Kussmaul sign, early ascites, hepatomegaly) with clear lungs, so prominent breathlessness argues against it.
Myocarditis gives chest pain, heart failure, arrhythmia and raised troponin; a rub means associated pericarditis. Cardiac MRI is the key test.
Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis and peaks at 5–15 years; it is rare under 3 and uncommon in adults.
Pericarditis: diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, then T inversion. Hyperacute T waves are the earliest sign of STEMI.
Fever, weight loss, a new regurgitant murmur and splinter haemorrhages is infective endocarditis: 3 sets of blood cultures before antibiotics, then echo.
Take ≥ 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics: they identify the organism and are a major Duke criterion; echo follows promptly.
Embolisation of vegetations, most often to the brain, makes new focal weakness an embolic stroke; image urgently and consider early surgery.
Surgery in IE: heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent bacteraemia, fungi) or large vegetations with emboli. Age is not an indication.
Constriction gives a raised JVP with rapid y descent, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock and ascites. Pulsus paradoxus is the hallmark of tamponade.
Right-sided congestion with a steep y descent after previous TB is constrictive pericarditis; CT/MRI shows thickening or calcification.
Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis weeks after MI (antimyocardial antibodies); treat with aspirin/NSAID plus colchicine.
Distant heart sounds with a newly enlarged globular silhouette after a viral illness is pericardial effusion (> 200–250 mL); echo confirms and checks for tamponade.
A to-and-fro scratchy sound in systole and diastole after a viral illness is a pericardial rub (acute viral pericarditis); treat with NSAID plus colchicine.
Acute pericarditis: high-dose aspirin or ibuprofen tapered over 1–2 weeks plus colchicine for 3 months (halves recurrence). Steroids are second line.
TB is the commonest cause of constriction worldwide; others are cardiac surgery, radiotherapy, viral/idiopathic pericarditis and connective tissue disease.
A large effusion in an older smoker suggests malignancy; a rub is often absent, echo confirms, and diuretics do not help. Drain and send cytology.
PR depression (with PR elevation in aVR) is the most specific ECG sign of pericarditis; ST elevation is diffuse, concave and without reciprocal change.
Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory SBP fall > 10 mmHg) is the key bedside sign that an effusion is causing tamponade; echo confirms.
Hypotension, distended neck veins and a water-bottle heart in lung cancer is malignant tamponade, so pulsus paradoxus is expected. Kussmaul sign suggests constriction.
Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression after a viral illness, no high-risk features: outpatient ibuprofen plus colchicine.
Pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward is acute pericarditis; with breast cancer consider malignant involvement and check echo.
Fever, pleuritic pain, rub and diffuse ST elevation weeks after MI is Dressler syndrome; early infarct pericarditis occurs within 1–3 days.
Fever and pleuritic pain 2 weeks after MI with no new ECG change is Dressler syndrome: aspirin/NSAID plus colchicine. Anticoagulation risks haemopericardium.
Chest discomfort, hypotension, raised JVP and quiet heart sounds hours after pacing suggest lead perforation with haemopericardium/tamponade.
Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds and low voltages weeks after MI is tamponade from a post-MI effusion: urgent echo and pericardiocentesis.
Multi-territory ST elevation with pleuritic pain in a young woman is pericarditis; a small troponin rise means myopericarditis, not ACS.
Carditis is the only rheumatic fever manifestation causing permanent damage (chronic rheumatic valve disease); arthritis, rash and chorea resolve.
MVP without regurgitation has near-population endocarditis risk. Prosthetic valves and previous IE carry the highest risk.
Viridans streptococcal native-valve IE is usually penicillin-sensitive with > 90% cure. S. aureus, prosthetic and culture-negative IE do worse.
Janeway lesions (painless palmar/plantar haemorrhagic macules from septic emboli) are characteristic of endocarditis; a minor Duke criterion.
After blood cultures, start empirical high-dose IV bactericidal antibiotics, then tailor to the organism for 4–6 weeks. Surgery only for specific indications.
Prolonged fever with a new wide pulse pressure suggests aortic valve endocarditis with acute AR; its soft short murmur is easily missed.
Jones minor criteria: fever, arthralgia, raised ESR/CRP, prolonged PR. Carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum and nodules are major.
Rheumatic arthritis responds dramatically to aspirin within 24–48 h; a rapid response supports the diagnosis.
An indolent illness with anaemia and partial response to antibiotics is subacute native-valve IE, classically viridans streptococci.
Microscopic haematuria (glomerulonephritis or renal emboli) is commoner in IE than splinters, Osler nodes or Roth spots; dipstick the urine.
A new or changing regurgitant murmur with fever is the most suggestive feature of IE; new regurgitation on echo is a major Duke criterion.
In people who inject drugs, S. aureus is the commonest cause of IE, usually tricuspid with septic pulmonary emboli; cover MRSA where prevalent.
Prophylaxis only for highest risk (prosthetic valves, previous IE, unrepaired cyanotic CHD). ASD, VSD, CABG and pacemakers do not qualify.
Immune-complex phenomena: Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis, rheumatoid factor. Splenic abscess is embolic (vascular), like Janeway lesions.
